docs.title: Kelp: what if we designed Git today?
docs.body: A blank-slate exploration of version control: keep the history, diffs, and useful merges, but rethink what a checkout contains and how one repository can grow across machines. What would Git look like if we designed it today, from scratch, without having to remain compatible with Git? That is the question I’m exploring with Kelp. I want the freedom to reconsider the foundations: what we download, what a commit represents, how independent contributions come together, and how a single repository can use more than one storage machine. At the same time, there is a lot I want to keep: useful diffs, intelligent merging, dependable history, local work, and the ability to recover a known state. This is an exercise in imagining a successor, with an early working implementation to test the ideas. To make sense of the choices, it helps to first understand what Git was built to do—and why its model has worked so well. Why Git exists Software changes constantly. We need to know what the files looked like before an edit, compare one version with another, recover from mistakes, and combine contributions from people working separately. Version control gives that work a recorded history. Git grew out of a particularly demanding version of this problem: developing the Linux kernel. Contributors were spread across the world, and many lines of development had to proceed in parallel. The kernel project began using BitKeeper, a proprietary distributed version-control system, in 2002. In 2005, the relationship between its developer and the Linux community broke down and free use was withdrawn. Linus Torvalds began developing Git to meet the project’s needs. The history in Pro Git describes the goals: speed, distributed work, strong support for parallel development, and efficient handling of a large project. So Git was never merely a way for one person to back up a few files. Collaboration and scale were part of the problem from the beginning. Its answer was to let people have their own repositories, work locally, and exchange recorded history. GitHub and other hosts later made a shared meeting place for that work convenient. Git is the version-control system underneath; a host adds things such as pull requests, discussions, permissions, and build automation. Now let’s put the machinery aside and picture how the basic idea works. Imagine a handbook with many authors Suppose a team maintains a technical handbook. It has pages about installation, operating services, handling incidents, and deploying releases. Several people edit it, and the team needs to know which advice appeared in each published edition. Think of a file as a page , a folder as a chapter , and the repository as the handbook together with its archive . When we make a Git commit, we record an edition of the handbook. The record says which version of every included page belongs in that edition, who recorded it, why, and which earlier edition or editions it follows. The collection of recorded file contents is a snapshot . There is no need to reprint every unchanged page. If the installation page is identical to the one already in the archive, the new edition can refer to that same stored page. Git’s fingerprints of stored contents make that reuse possible. Suppose we clarify a page about retrying failed requests. A diff shows what changed: The minus line was removed; the plus line was added. This tells a reviewer something much more useful than “there is a new edition.” To record that edit in Git: git add selects the contents for the next commit. In our handbook, it puts the chosen revised page on an editor’s tray. git commit records the edition assembled from that selection. This separation is useful: I can include a correction while leaving another unfinished edit on my desk. It also means the draft page, the page on the tray, and the last recorded page can differ. Git calls those the working copy, staging area, and committed version. That is already a powerful tool: exact editions, explanations for changes, and a way to compare them. Take a copy and try a different direction A normal full clone is like taking home a copy of the handbook and its available archive. I can inspect the history and record new editions without staying connected to a central library. A branch is a movable bookmark in that history. A bookmark called main might point to the edition the team works from, while another bookmark follows my unfinished revision. Moving a bookmark is cheap; making a branch does not require physically copying all the pages again. Two authors can start from the same edition and work independently. One improves the retry guidance, while another corrects the installation instructions. Git can compare both with their common starting edition and usually combine edits to different pages automatically. That is the basic idea of a three-way merge : look at the shared starting point and at what each person changed. If both replace the same sentence with incompatible instructions, the tool asks for a decision instead of guessing. We can send our recorded work to another repository with a push , and fetch work from it. In practice, teams often gather around a shared host, but the useful local copy remains ours. I would want to retain all of this in a successor. These are not incidental conveniences. They are why version control makes experimentation and collaboration manageable. What happens when the handbook becomes a library? Now imagine that handbook has grown into many volumes. Different teams maintain different chapters. The archive contains years of revisions and large diagrams. Some readers need the whole collection; others need one page to complete a small task. A modern codebase can have the same shape: applications, services, shared libraries, generated assets, infrastructure, and documentation kept in one repository. Keeping them together is useful when a change needs to update several parts at once. But it also exposes questions that are less noticeable in a small project. How much do I need to take home? A developer working on a single service may need only a small part of the repository. A short-lived build environment or coding agent may spend significant time acquiring data before doing a comparatively small amount of work. Git has real answers here. A sparse checkout limits which pages are laid out on the desk. A partial clone can leave some stored contents at the library and retrieve them when needed. Those are different choices: which files appear in the working folder, and which contents are stored locally. Git’s partial-clone design documents both the benefits and the consequences of needing missing data later. Which version did I actually save? If I put a revised page on the staging tray and then edit it again on my desk, the tray still holds the earlier contents. Tests may run against my latest draft while the next commit records the selected version. Each distinction has a purpose, but it is extra bookkeeping for a person—or an agent—trying to answer a simpler question: what am I about to share? How much history needs to be reconciled? Suppose two authors independently revise different pages and both want to update the shared main bookmark. One gets there first. The other cannot simply replace it with their own edition, because that edition doesn’t include the first person’s work. Git correctly protects against that update. The second author can merge, keeping both original commits, or rebase their work onto the newer starting point. Separate branches let both publish independently, with integration happening later. But combining work is still expressed through relationships between project-wide recorded editions. Where does the growing library live? A host can put different repositories on different servers. It can keep several copies of a busy repository to serve more readers. Splitting the storage and write workload of one large repository is a further problem, requiring infrastructure beyond simply placing Git on another machine. AI makes these questions more immediate. Agents can create many parallel attempts, often in disposable workspaces. Continuous integration repeatedly needs exact source inputs. The cost of preparing a workspace or updating shared state can be paid far more often than an individual developer sees in their terminal. The point is not that Git cannot support these workflows. It does. The question is which assumptions we would choose if those workflows were central to a fresh design. More shelves, more copies, and a lot of coordination There are two easy-to-confuse forms of distribution in the handbook analogy. Giving every author an independent copy is like Git’s distributed development model. Operating one library across several buildings is a hosting problem. Solving the first does not automatically solve the second. A bigger server is a taller bookcase: more capacity, eventually with physical or economic limits. Horizontal scaling means adding machines and sharing the storage or work among them. Extra complete copies can help more people read at once. But those copies need to stay sufficiently current, and somebody still has to determine which updates have been accepted. GitLab’s Gitaly Cluster documentation describes a case where replicas lag behind a heavily updated repository, leaving the primary to serve most or all of the reads. There is also maintenance. Git packages and compresses stored objects into packfiles . Serving history and keeping those packs efficient involves real computation. GitHub’s work on monorepo maintenance shows how much can be improved by indexing multiple packs and concentrating more maintenance on recent additions. Recent systems move the durable archive away from the serving machines. Cursor’s Continuity design, published in August 2026, uses a write-ahead log in object storage: a durable journal of pushes, with an index governing which entries have been published. Local Git repositories become serving copies that can be rebuilt and brought up to date from that record. In our library, the journal and archived pages outlive any particular reading room. More reading rooms can be opened without making each one an irreplaceable source of truth. The published log still needs an agreed order, and the stored data still needs maintenance. GitLab’s June 2026 scaling proposal explores a related separation between authoritative object storage and local caches. Meta’s Mononoke architecture is another important example of separating saved contents from changing records. This is work I want to learn from. Git compatibility is valuable: existing clients and tools keep working. But maintaining that compatibility also constrains what can change underneath the interface. Kelp gives me permission to ask a different question: what if the editing model, checkout model, and storage model could all be designed together? Start with a blank sheet For this experiment, I don’t have to preserve Git’s object model or speak its network protocol. I can keep the useful behavior while reconsidering how it is represented. Returning to the handbook: does every contribution need to be recorded as a new edition of the entire book? Or could the primary record describe the pages being changed and the earlier versions of those pages it replaces? Imagine an editor submitting a change slip: “replace the retry page I worked from with these revised contents.” Someone correcting installation.md can submit another slip. Both refer to the earlier pages they actually used. Neither needs to be rewritten merely because the other slip arrived first. That is the idea behind a Kelp commit . Internally, it is an edit transaction : one record containing a batch of file edits. Each edit identifies the preceding version or versions of that path and its new contents, or an explicit deletion. These are file-level relationships; the record is not just the displayed line diff. With both corrections, the handbook contains the revised retry guidance and the corrected installation instructions. The same two saved edits produce that result whichever arrives first; neither edit needs to be rewritten. The practical benefit is that I can finish and share my page correction without first integrating an unrelated correction just because it reached the shared host earlier. Work that actually overlaps still needs a decision, as we’ll see in the merging example. This draws on a long line of work around changes and dependencies, including Pijul and Darcs. I’m exploring a particular combination of file-scoped transactions, local workflows, and partitioned storage. I’m not claiming that changes as a primary concept are new. Keep related pages in the same envelope Some edits are independent; others need to travel together. Suppose the handbook’s installation page refers to a setup script, and we rename that script. Updating only the prose would leave a broken instruction. Updating only the script would leave readers following the old name. The change slip should contain the whole operation: the revised instruction, the old script’s removal, and the new script’s contents. In Kelp, one transaction can record all of those file edits together. Before the remote publishes that transaction, it checks that the required contents and earlier transactions are available. A reader includes the entire record, not whichever half happened to be easiest to download first. This also applies to later dependencies. If another edit builds on a file version created by that multi-file transaction, it needs that transaction’s complete logical context. I can therefore preserve a coordinated change without requiring unrelated pages to acquire dependencies on it. In software, that matters for changes such as updating an API and its callers together. The tool cannot discover every semantic relationship in the code. Two separate files can still interact badly at runtime. Choosing the right unit of work, reviewing it, and testing the result remain necessary. Take home one page, or one chapter Once work has explicit file-level dependencies, a small checkout becomes a natural part of the model. In the handbook, I want to take home the retry page and enough history to work on it correctly. I don’t need all the installation diagrams or every unrelated chapter’s changes. With a Kelp remote configured by its operator, I can select an individual file: Or I can select several files and directories: These are alternative examples using a placeholder server. --paths accepts project-relative files and directory prefixes, not glob patterns. The selected scope is remembered for commits, pulls, and restores. The key rule is that a page absent from my desk is not a page I deleted from the handbook. Files outside the selection are not downloaded or treated as deletions. A file I create outside the selection stays local. Kelp retrieves relevant transactions and their complete dependencies, along with the historical contents for selected paths. A multi-file transaction retains its full description and original identity even when some of its file contents remain on the remote. Selection changes what is materialized, not what the original author’s commit meant. If I discover I need another chapter, I can expand the checkout: In a software project, the selection must still include what its build and tests require. Kelp cannot infer all those dependencies for me. Nor is a partial checkout a complete backup or a permissions boundary. It is a deliberate choice about which data I need locally. Save, inspect, and share deliberately The ordinary workflow can remain familiar even though the record underneath it is different. After editing the selected retry page: diff lets me inspect the edit. commit saves the included file changes locally. push shares committed work, leaving later unfinished edits on my machine. New files within the selected scope are included automatically unless ignore rules exclude them. There is no separate staging tray in this workflow. Saving a version is an explicit decision, and sharing it is another. I can also start a project locally with kelp init, without an account or remote. A failed push leaves committed work queued under its original identity, so retrying doesn’t silently create a new commit from whatever is on my desk at that moment. Meanwhile, another author can share an edit to the installation page. The remote validates each contribution’s actual dependencies. It does not reject my unrelated page correction because the other person advanced a project-wide bookmark first. That changes where coordination is needed. We can collect independent contributions while leaving the decision about which combined state to release as a separate concern. Keep the useful intelligence in merging A new model should not make people manually combine changes that a tool can sensibly reconcile. Suppose the original retry page contains three paragraphs: One author clarifies which failures should be retried. Another independently improves the delay guidance. A combined diff would include both edits: Both can fit on the same page. Kelp uses the common file ancestor to attempt a three-way text merge, including when there are unfinished local edits to preserve. The original transactions remain available; the combined result is committed explicitly when ready. Now imagine both authors replace the first paragraph, one with “Retry transient failures” and the other with “Never retry automatically.” That is a disagreement about policy. There is no correct answer hidden in which upload arrived last. Kelp keeps both alternatives. An existing contributor can choose a starting side, edit it into the intended result, and record the resolution: The side choice changes the working file. The resolution commit records both preceding alternatives as parents, even if the final contents match one of them unchanged. Both original contributions remain inspectable. This is also a limit of the promise. Competing binary files or a file-versus-directory collision need explicit handling, and an unresolved conflict affecting selected files can prevent a new clone from materializing them. Retaining disagreement is valuable, but the interface still has to help people make the decision. Publish an exact edition when you need one Our handbook still needs editions. A release cannot mean “whatever combination of pages each reader happened to collect.” Kelp constructs a view from a selected set of transactions and all the earlier work they require. In the analogy, this is an edition assembled from a specified collection of change slips. Given the same complete set, clients can derive the same file alternatives. A conflict-free result identifies exact project contents. A saved view records files and their transaction context for recovery. A release tag can give a complete, committed saved view a memorable name. From a full checkout of the committed state I want to identify: The name is immutable: it cannot later be moved to a different view. If separate contributors independently use the same name for different views, both are retained and the exact view identifier is needed to distinguish them. This does not make a tag an approval or a test result. It gives those processes something exact to refer to. A team’s protected integration policy still needs coordination; Kelp does not claim that merely storing all contributions produces a tested release. History remains useful at two levels: One tells me which states this checkout saved. The other tells me which pieces of work it contains. kelp show can inspect either kind using its hash—a fingerprint, normally displayed as a short unambiguous prefix. To recover the tagged edition: Restore first records a labelled backup of the current included files, then restores in place. The output gives the backup’s view hash so I can get back to my previous work. A partial recovery view retains its original scope, even if I expanded the checkout afterwards. These recovery records are not automatically shared commits. To share a restored result, I deliberately commit and push it. History journaling, inspection, and recovery remain part of the experience rather than being sacrificed to the different collaboration model. Put the archive across several buildings The handbook can now be assembled from independent records while still supporting exact editions. That gives the hosting design different units to work with. In Kelp’s distributed deployment, gateways receive requests, validate contributions, and route them to storage nodes . The nodes hold portions of the same project’s contents and journals of its transactions. Think of several library buildings, each storing part of the archive, with additional copies for resilience. A visitor uses a counter that knows how to find the records. The counter does not need to own the one master bookmark through which every independent correction must pass. File contents are stored before the transaction describing their edits is published. The required dependencies and replicated contents are checked, then a complete transaction record makes the whole batch discoverable. Another gateway accepting an unrelated commit does not invalidate it. Pull combines records discovered from the nodes’ journals and retrieves missing dependencies before constructing a view. Duplicate records identify the same work and do not apply it twice. Journal positions help a client resume transfer; they are not a global ordering of everyone’s contributions. The result is an exact set of observed work, not a promise that every node was read at the same universal “latest instant.” An immutable view is how I state the particular edition I mean. The distributed implementation defaults to two durable copies of objects, journal entries, and release pins on distinct storage nodes. With three nodes and two copies, reads and writes can continue with one node unavailable. Too many missing journals cause an error rather than a misleading claim that the absent data doesn’t exist. Repair and evacuation let operators restore replica placement or move data off a retiring node. Commit identities stay the same when storage placement changes. Gateways need a consistent membership configuration to discover the same nodes. The goal is for adding machines to help one project , rather than only making room for another repository. Physical partitioning and node-failure behavior are implemented and tested. Linear performance scaling is still something to measure, not something I can infer from the diagram. Each node still serializes its own database writes, and validation, discovery, and large views have costs. What the clean slate buys—and what it costs The freedom to choose a new model lets these ideas fit together: take one page or chapter, record edits with narrow dependencies, combine independent work, preserve conflicts, name exact editions, and distribute the stored records. There are practical file concerns too. Large files use reusable chunks, symlinks retain their targets, and native filenames are preserved on filesystems that can represent them. kelp gc compacts physical storage while retaining logical commits, conflicts, saved views, and recovery backups. But a clean slate is not a free upgrade. Git’s existing ecosystem is an enormous advantage. Kelp has its own format and protocol. Git import can preserve committed history, merge results, modes, symlinks, tags, and original commit information, but that is not the same thing as complete two-way Git compatibility. External LFS contents and submodule projects remain separate concerns. There are also measured costs. In a recorded development fixture with 1,000 repetitive 4 KiB files and 100 single-file edits, compaction left Kelp slightly smaller than maintained Git: 323,584 versus 330,148 bytes. Kelp’s status and initial capture were slower. The benchmark notes explain the workload, persistence differences, and trade-offs. Those development results are not a blanket claim about current-release performance. The current implementation is 0.0.4. Per-file and directory checkouts, independent transactions, text merging, saved views, large-file chunks, replicated storage, and Git import are working parts of it. There is more to do on very large histories, richer conflict tools, author signatures, finer-grained access control, and review or CI policy around selected views. The question that matters to me is whether the freedom to redesign those foundations can produce a better overall experience. Can a person—or an agent—work on the part they need, share it predictably, and recover confidently? Can a repository grow across machines while remaining one understandable project? That is what I mean by reimagining Git today. Start with the job version control needs to do, keep the parts that make it valuable, and give ourselves permission to choose a different shape for the rest. Notes and sources The handbook is an analogy for files, snapshots, branches, dependencies, and storage. The diffs and diagrams are illustrative examples. This article describes my Kelp 0.0.4 implementation, inspected on 25 September 2026. - Pro Git: a short history of Git - Pro Git: snapshots, local operations, and the staging area - Kelp’s commands and current behavior - My transaction and view design - Distribution and its consistency boundaries - Research and prior art

docs.title: jsql: asking SQL questions of JSON
docs.body: A small, fast way for me—and the coding agents I work with—to ask SQL questions of JSON. Exploring a predictable shell interface, native execution, and the choices that connect the two formats. Imagine downloading a JSON export of some orders. You want to know which region brought in the most paid revenue. The data is already on your computer. You don’t need to build an application around it; you just want an answer. I can picture the SQL almost immediately: keep the paid orders, group them by region, and add up their amounts. But the data is sitting in a JSON file, not a database table. jsql is my experiment in closing that gap. Feed it JSON, give it a SQL query, and get JSON back. It is a small command-line tool built around SQLite, with a TypeScript entry point compiled into a standalone executable. I wanted it to be easy for coding agents to use too. An agent often needs to inspect data before deciding what to do next. A familiar query language and a predictable result format give it a direct way to ask for what it needs. That was one of the motivations alongside making my own shell work easier and keeping the command fast. The command looks simple. Most of the design work sits underneath it: deciding what counts as a row, what happens to nested values, and how to get from the input to a useful result without unnecessary preparation. Start with a question about some data JSON is a way to represent structured data as text. An object groups named values, such as an order’s ID and amount. An array is a list of values. A list of objects often looks a lot like a table waiting to happen. Here is the example we’ll use. Save it as orders.json: We could read four records by eye. The same approach becomes tedious with thousands of them, especially when the question changes: which orders are large, how many are paid, or what is the total for each region? SQL is a language for asking questions of tables. SELECT chooses the values to return, WHERE chooses the rows, and ORDER BY chooses the result order. If I already know those operations, I want to use that knowledge directly. With jsql installed, I can ask for paid orders worth at least 100: The result is: data is the name jsql gives the input. The shell’s < orders.json sends the file to the program. There is no database connection string or import command to arrange first. The paid = 1 deserves an explanation: jsql exposes JSON true and false as SQLite’s integer values 1 and 0. That is one of the choices needed to make the two data models meet. Keep the command small enough to compose There are already good ways to work with JSON. jq has a language built around transforming it. DuckDB can query JSON directly and supports much broader analytical workflows. SQLite itself has extensive JSON functions. I’m exploring a particular shape of tool: one SQL query as an argument, one JSON document on input, and a JSON array on output. The convenience is in that small contract. The original revenue question becomes: GROUP BY region gathers each region’s rows together. sum(amount) adds their amounts. AS total gives the result a useful name. The unpaid order is left out before the totals are calculated. Because the answer is JSON too, another invocation can consume it. Here is a deliberately simple two-stage pipeline: select the paid orders, then count them. The connects one program’s output to the next program’s input. I could express that count in one query, but the example shows why the output format matters. The result stays usable as data rather than becoming a decorated table intended only for a person to read. Normal output goes to standard output, the stream a pipe consumes. Error messages go to standard error, and failures return exit code 1. Successful results are compact JSON followed by a newline. Those small choices make the tool fit into a shell workflow. Make the interface useful to an agent An agent investigating those orders has the same question I do, but I don’t want it to need the entire export in its conversation. It can ask the query engine to do the filtering and arithmetic, then read the small result it needs for the next decision. In the revenue example, that means two totals come back instead of every order. SQL supplies the vocabulary for the question; JSON supplies a structured answer. The agent can inspect it, refine the query, or pass it to another command without first producing a separate data-processing script. That influenced the command’s shape. It has one query argument, a known input name, machine-readable output, and an exit status that says whether execution succeeded. An agent must check that status before treating the output as a result. A syntax error should lead to correcting the query, not interpreting an error message as data. The query still needs to express the right question. Forgetting WHERE paid = 1 would produce a valid answer to the wrong revenue calculation. Likewise, SELECT can still return far more data than the agent needs. The useful behavior comes from selecting the relevant columns and rows, not merely from placing a tool between the model and a file. Ease of use here is something I can evaluate: can an agent get to the correct answer with a short, understandable sequence of commands? Query speed matters too, especially when that sequence starts the executable repeatedly. Decide what a row means The first mapping is straightforward: each element of an input array becomes a row, and object keys become columns. A single object becomes one row. But JSON objects do not all have to contain the same keys. If the first record has a name and the second also has a team, looking only at the first record would lose a column. So jsql discovers keys across the input. Consider: For SELECT name, team FROM data ORDER BY name, the result is: Missing fields become SQL NULL, meaning an absent or unknown value. An explicit JSON null maps to the same SQL value. That makes a useful rectangular view of uneven records, but it also means the exposed column alone does not distinguish “missing” from “explicitly null.” For a field that can be missing, the SQL test is IS NULL. For example, given this separate input: The query SELECT id, discount FROM data WHERE discount IS NULL ORDER BY id returns: Column names need care as well. JSON permits names containing spaces or words SQL uses for other purposes. Quoting the name lets me ask for it directly: And an array doesn’t have to contain objects at all. For a list of scalar values—individual numbers, strings, or booleans—jsql provides a column called value: An empty array produces no rows. The goal of these conventions is that small differences in input shape have explainable consequences, without requiring a schema file alongside every export. Keep nested data explicit Our orders include a customer object. What should a table column contain when the original value has a structure of its own? I chose to expose nested objects and arrays as JSON text. The top level becomes columns; deeper structure stays available through SQLite’s JSON functions. To extract the city from the first two orders: The path $.city means “the city property at the root of this JSON value.” json extract reads it and returns the corresponding SQL value. There is an important consequence when selecting the entire nested value: That result contains a string holding JSON , not a nested object. The escaped quotation marks show the difference. Likewise, selecting paid directly returns 1 or 0, not a JSON boolean. This is a query result expressed as JSON, with SQLite’s value types in between. It is not a promise that SELECT will round-trip every aspect of the original document unchanged. Keeping that distinction visible is more useful than making the interface appear lossless when it isn’t. Let SQLite do the querying At this point, the temptation might be to implement a small SQL-like language over JavaScript arrays. A basic filter would be easy enough. Grouping, sorting, null handling, expressions, and all the interactions between them would quickly become their own project. I used SQLite as the query engine. It runs inside jsql’s process, so the person using the command does not need to start a database server. The current implementation has three parts: The TypeScript entry point is intentionally small. It checks the arguments, handles help, reads standard input, and passes the document and query to the bridge. Inside the bridge, SQLite first validates the input as one strict JSON document and retains it in its JSONB representation. That is SQLite’s internal binary representation of parsed JSON. It lets JSON operations work with the parsed structure without repeatedly converting the same text. It is not the JSONB format used by PostgreSQL. jsql then discovers the row keys and creates a view called data. A view is a query exposed under a table-like name. Here it reads from SQLite’s jsonb each function and extracts the named fields; jsql does not first insert every input row into a separate ordinary table. I also kept the discovery pass focused on keys. After SQLite has validated the document, a small scanner finds the top-level property names used by its rows. Each distinct spelling is decoded through SQLite, including escaped names. That avoids asking SQLite’s general-purpose row machinery to repeatedly rediscover the same schema across a large input. There is still work proportional to the input. A LIMIT 1 query does not eliminate the initial read and schema discovery. The benefit is removing unnecessary work between “I have JSON” and “SQLite can query it.” Make the executable easy to carry Using TypeScript for the entry point does not mean the installed command needs a JavaScript runtime alongside it. I used scriptc to compile the entry point into a native executable, with a small foreign-function interface to the C bridge. That interface is the connection that lets the TypeScript function call reach the SQLite code. SQLite is included in the build. The build uses Node.js, Bun, Clang, and a pinned SQLite source archive. It verifies that archive against a recorded checksum before compiling it, so the query engine is a deliberate build input rather than whichever SQLite happens to be installed on the machine. Those are build requirements. The resulting jsql executable runs without a separate Node.js, Bun, SQLite installation, or npm dependency tree. The size I recorded for the macOS ARM64 build is about 1.1 MiB. This fits the kind of tool I wanted: something small enough to install and reach for when a file lands in my terminal. With Binzo installed, the release can be installed with: The release downloads cover macOS and Linux on x64 and ARM64. The contributor guide explains building it locally. Turn a working binary into a usable tool Getting an answer on my own machine was only part of the job. The TypeScript entry point, the native bridge, and SQLite have to agree about the data crossing between them. Then someone else has to be able to obtain an executable that works on their machine too. I made the tests run the compiled command. The test helper starts a child process, pipes JSON into it, and reads the output. That exercises the interface a user actually sees, including argument handling and the trip through the native bridge. The cases are small but deliberate: a key appearing only in a later record, a property name containing a quotation mark, nested JSON returning as text, and strings containing newlines or an emoji. These are places where “JSON in, JSON out” needs a more precise definition. I wanted the tests focused on those choices rather than trying to retest SQLite’s entire SQL language. The first implementation commit, on 14 September, included those tests, the benchmark, and the release workflow together. The workflow builds on the target operating systems and architectures and runs checks before publishing the four platform archives. A locally successful build is not treated as proof that the other targets work. The next step was making the route into the tool shorter. Later that day, I added the Binzo installation instructions. Instead of starting every reader with Node, Bun, and a C compiler, the README could lead with downloading a suitable release and running a query. That connects the two projects neatly: jsql concentrates on querying the data; Binzo handles getting the right executable onto the machine. On 15 September, I added the MIT licence and updated the archive packaging to include it. The permission to use and redistribute the tool belongs alongside the distributed binary, not only on its repository page. Those follow-up changes didn’t add another SQL feature. They made the thing I had built easier to try, check, and share. For a small command-line tool, that is part of whether the idea becomes useful. Measure the whole command For a short-lived shell tool, the query engine’s execution time is only part of the experience. Starting the program, reading the input, and writing the answer all count. I also tested and benchmarked jsql against jq. In many of the cases I tried, jsql was faster. That was an encouraging part of the experiment: the SQL-shaped interface I wanted for myself and for agents could also perform well on those workloads. The result depends on the operation and input, so I treat it as a finding from those comparisons rather than a claim about every JSON task. The benchmark script I checked into the repository measures jsql itself. It launches fresh processes with piped input and output, and checks each answer against an expected result outside the timed section. It measures startup, filtering, grouping, sorting, and full output separately. The contributor notes also make the comparison conditions explicit: run on the same machine, account for warm caches, and look at the child process’s peak memory as well as elapsed time. The figures I recorded in the README were measured on an Apple M4 Max running macOS ARM64, using scriptc 0.0.36. They are medians of seven runs after two warmups: - For 100,000 rows, 7.22 MiB of input , filtering with a limit took 23 ms, grouping and summing took 58 ms, and returning the full data took 80 ms. - For 1,000,000 rows, 74.07 MiB of input , those measurements were 193 ms, 821 ms, and 794 ms respectively. These timings are for jsql alone; they do not quantify its advantage over jq. A wide record, a large nested value, or a different query can change what dominates the run. Output is buffered in 64 KiB chunks, so jsql does not need to construct one enormous result string before writing it. Input is different: the original JSON and its binary representation are held in memory, and sorting or grouping can need additional memory. This is not a streaming-input engine for an arbitrarily large file. The number model has limits too. SQLite uses signed 64-bit integers and double-precision floating-point values. That matters if the input contains numbers whose precision needs to be preserved beyond those representations. What I want to keep simple The current boundary is deliberately small: one JSON document, one query argument, and one JSON array result. Newline-delimited JSON—separate JSON documents on successive lines—is not the same input format. I want to learn where that boundary is useful and where it becomes an obstacle. How often do the straightforward top-level columns answer the question? When does nested JSON need more help? Are the type conversions obvious enough from the output? Can an agent recognise and recover from a query error without a long detour? Does a faster command translate into a better overall investigation? There are much larger data tools available, and I don’t need jsql to grow into all of them. The useful outcome here is smaller: when I have JSON and can already express my question in SQL, the step between the two should be short. Notes and further reading This article describes my implementation at 24 September 2026, which embeds SQLite 3.51.0. The orders are invented example data; the query outputs shown here were checked against the macOS ARM64 release. - The command-line entry point - JSON mapping, the SQLite bridge, and output buffering - Tests for uneven records, nested values, and scalar rows - The pinned build and native compilation - SQLite’s JSON functions and JSONB format

docs.title: Binzo: from a release download to a command
docs.body: A project publishes a binary. I want to run it and keep it updated. Exploring the small decisions between those two things, from choosing a download to recovering an interrupted update. A project publishes a command-line tool. I open its releases page and find a list of downloads: different operating systems, different processors, a few compressed formats, and perhaps some files whose purpose is less obvious. Somewhere in that list is the program I want. I need to choose it, unpack it, find the executable, put it somewhere my terminal can find it, and remember how I installed it when an update arrives. None of those steps is especially remarkable on its own. Together, they are a repeated little maintenance job. Binzo is my attempt to turn that job into a consistent workflow. Give it a repository, let it resolve a published release, and install a command from the release’s downloads. Later, ask it to update the tools it remembers. The surface is small: The interesting question is what Binzo has to know, and what it should ask me, for those commands to be dependable. Start with the files a project already publishes A source-code repository and an installable program are different things. The repository may contain everything needed to build a tool, but I may just want the already-built result. On GitHub, a release is a published version with notes and downloadable assets . An asset might be a ready-to-run executable, an archive containing one, or a checksum file. GitHub also provides source-code archives. Its release documentation explains the distinction. Package managers can already handle installation and updates well. The gap I wanted to explore is a tool that has suitable release downloads, where I want to use those downloads directly without first writing a package definition for each project. For the built-in GitHub provider, binzo add owner/repo goes to GitHub’s release API. With no tag specified, it asks for GitHub’s latest published stable release. An explicit tag selects that release instead, including a prerelease: add and install are aliases. The tag has to correspond to a published release; the existence of a Git tag alone doesn’t imply there is a binary available to install. That removes the first manual step: finding the release. Choosing a file from it is a separate problem. Work out which download fits this machine Take a release with these filenames. These are the platform names used by jsql’s downloads: On an Apple Silicon Mac, the intended download is jsql-macos-arm64.tar.gz. macos describes the operating system, arm64 describes the processor architecture, and .tar.gz describes the archive format. SHA256SUMS contains checksums; it is not the program. The difficulty is that projects don’t all use those words. Another project might write darwin for macOS or aarch64 for ARM64. An Intel or AMD 64-bit build might be labelled x64, amd64, or x86 64. I built the matcher around common aliases and filename tokens. It checks the operating system and architecture, excludes known incompatible candidates, and prefers a clearly matching download. Longer aliases are recognised first so that arm64 isn’t also mistaken for the shorter arm label. Linux adds another wrinkle. Some binaries target glibc , while others target musl —different implementations of a basic system library programs can depend on. On a musl system, Binzo excludes downloads it recognises as glibc-only. The processor name alone is not always enough to choose a runnable program. These checks use the filenames supplied by the publisher. They reduce the work of choosing, but they cannot establish every runtime requirement from a name. The project still needs to publish an appropriate binary for the machine. Let uncertainty become a question Suppose a project publishes both a standard build and a specialised build for the same platform. Or the filename says only tool.zip, with no platform information at all. Picking the first file in the list would turn an unclear situation into an invisible guess. I made Binzo ask when the choice is ambiguous or the target is uncertain. Some differences don’t need a question. If the same filename stem appears as both .tar.gz and .zip, Binzo treats those as equivalent packaging choices and prefers .tar.gz. Different variants still remain separate choices. For unattended use, the same decisions can be made explicit. Here is an illustrative command for a project whose release contains that archive and executable: Each option answers a different question: - --asset names the exact uploaded file to download. - --binary names the executable’s relative path inside the unpacked archive. - --name chooses the command I will type. The asset option is an exact filename, not a URL or pattern. If an unattended run can’t make the necessary choices, it reports what is available and which option would resolve the ambiguity. It should not hang waiting for a menu nobody can see. This is a recurring design choice in Binzo: make the ordinary path short, but keep the underlying decisions available when the automatic answer is incomplete. Find the program inside the download Downloading the right archive still doesn’t tell me which file to run. A release might contain a README, licences, supporting data, and more than one executable. Treating every file without an extension as a program would make ordinary documentation look installable. Binzo inspects files for executable headers or a Unix shebang , the first line that tells the system which interpreter should run a script. It does this without running the downloaded code. Desktop application bundles are excluded from command-line discovery. If the archive has one suitable executable, the choice is straightforward. If it has several, Binzo asks which one I want. On an update, it first tries to find the executable path I used before, then an unambiguous filename match. I keep the extracted support files alongside the executable. Copying only the apparent main program out of an archive can break a tool that expects data beside it. The current implementation accepts standalone executables and common archives such as tar, gzip, and ZIP. XZ and bzip2 formats need their corresponding extraction utilities. It excludes operating-system installer packages such as .dmg, .deb, and .msi; running a full system installer is a different workflow. It also doesn’t resolve an installed tool’s native library dependencies. If a release needs system libraries that aren’t present, that remains part of the project’s installation requirements. Give the command a stable place to live Once the files are ready, I need to be able to type the command without remembering its full path. The shell finds commands through PATH : a list of directories it searches. Binzo keeps the installations in one place and exposes commands through another: On Unix systems, the command is a symlink—a filesystem link—to the executable inside its installation. On Windows, Binzo creates a .cmd launcher, so exposing the command doesn’t require administrator permission to make symlinks. The tracking record ties together the registry, repository, release tag, asset, executable path, and chosen command name. That is the information an update needs. One executable is tracked for each repository within a registry. Command names can collide. If another tool already owns a name, Binzo asks for another name or reports the conflict. If the shell would find a different installation earlier on PATH, it reports that too. “The file was installed” and “typing the command runs this file” are not always the same thing. Binzo can configure zsh, bash, fish, or the Windows user PATH. But an installer cannot change the environment of the terminal that launched it. When necessary, it prints the command to update the current terminal; new terminals pick up the saved shell configuration. --no-modify-path keeps that configuration step manual. Those details are mundane, but they decide whether installation actually feels finished. An update has to remember the original choice The reason to track installations becomes clearer when the next release appears: Binzo remembers the asset variant and executable selected earlier, so a routine update can follow the same choice. If a release reorganises its downloads and that choice can no longer be identified unambiguously, it asks again. There is an important distinction around versions. Installing with @v0.0.1 selects that initial version. It does not pin future updates to it. A normal update moves the installation to latest. To explicitly switch an already-installed tool to a particular release: For update --all, a download or selection failure in one tool does not have to prevent every other tool from being considered. Binzo reports totals and returns an unsuccessful exit status if any tool failed. If installation recovery itself is blocked, it stops before modifying more tools. That last case needs more than a helpful message. It needs a way to know what happened halfway through an update. Prepare the replacement before switching over Imagine replacing the current executable in place while a new download is arriving. If the connection fails or the process stops at the wrong point, I might be left with neither a usable old version nor a complete new one. I made installation prepare a separate replacement first: For GitHub downloads, Binzo checks the expected size and verifies the SHA-256 digest when GitHub supplies one. A digest is a fingerprint of the downloaded contents; comparing it checks that the received file matches the expected bytes. It does not tell us whether the program itself is well behaved. The more subtle problem is that switching the command and saving installed.json are separate operations. An atomic rename can replace an individual file without exposing a half-written version, but it does not make the entire sequence one indivisible action. So I added a recovery journal : a small record describing the previous and proposed installations before the switch starts. Saving the new tracking state is the commit point—the point Binzo treats as completing the change. If interrupted before that state is saved, recovery restores the previous installation. If the new state was saved, recovery finishes the remaining cleanup. The previous package stays available until the replacement is committed. This is recovery from an interrupted change, not a permanent archive of all installed versions. After a successful update, Binzo normally cleans up the old installation. A lock also prevents two installs from overwriting each other’s tracking changes. Binzo can wait for a running installation or recover an abandoned one. For scripts, those choices are available as --wait and --recover; neither terminates a running process. These are the parts that make an installer more than a download shortcut. The useful promise is being able to explain which installation owns the command, including after something goes wrong. Keep release lookup separate from installation GitHub is the built-in source, but I didn’t want every installation step to depend on GitHub’s particular API response. The code separates a provider —the part that resolves releases and downloads assets—from the common pipeline for matching, extraction, selection, and tracking. A release provider supplies a small set of useful facts: the tag, release page, asset names, download references, and available size or digest information. Once Binzo has those facts, it can use the same installation machinery. There is also an adapter for declarative registries. A configuration can point at a definition describing how to find versions and assets in another JSON API. For example: Then an installation can select that registry by its configured name: Custom definitions use jq expressions to turn API responses into versions and assets, so that adapter requires jq. The built-in GitHub provider does not. Definitions need to return versions newest first; Binzo doesn’t assume every project uses the same version-number scheme. This gives other release services a way in without making each of them reimplement command ownership, updates, and recovery. Make Binzo itself straightforward to install There is a slightly circular problem in building an installer: people still need to install the installer. I added an npm distribution path: This requires Node.js 20 or newer during installation. npm selects the platform-specific binary package, including the Linux library variant. A one-time install script places that executable at the command path. Running binzo then launches the standalone executable directly. There is no separate Node launcher process on every invocation, and the user does not need Bun installed. Binzo’s development and executable build use Bun; the downloaded tools keep their own implementation and runtime requirements. The release workflow builds macOS, Linux, and Windows variants for x64 and ARM64, including both glibc and musl Linux variants. The small npm wrapper and the binary packages are published separately, with matching versions. I like that this connects to the other tools I’m building. jsql can publish a compact executable and let Binzo handle choosing and placing it. Tuna can use the same installation route. Neither needs Binzo to understand its internal implementation. What I want to keep learning The current tool implements GitHub release lookup, platform matching, interactive selection, tracked installation, updates, recovery, and custom registry support. My tests exercise failures after a command link has changed, interrupted transactions, and cases where an unrelated file occupies a command path. Other tests cover matching and archive handling without downloading or executing third-party tools. The open-ended part is the variety of real release layouts. How often can Binzo make a confident choice? When does a question save time, and when is it asking about a packaging detail it should handle itself? How well do remembered choices survive a project changing its release process? I also want failure messages to leave me with a clear next step. A missing release, an ambiguous asset, an unavailable system dependency, and a blocked recovery are different situations. Treating all of them as “installation failed” would leave most of the original maintenance job with the user. The idea remains a practical one: take the release files a project already publishes and make installing and updating them an understandable, repeatable operation. Notes and further reading This write-up describes my implementation at 24 September 2026. The jsql filenames come from its published release; the owner/tool and custom-registry examples are illustrative. - Installation and command reference - Platform matching and ambiguous assets - Selecting and installing an executable - Tracking, the commit point, and recovery - GitHub release lookup and digest verification - The npm installation bridge

docs.title: Tuna: making feedback outlast the conversation
docs.body: I correct an agent, it adjusts, and next time I may have to explain it again. Exploring how those corrections could become useful instructions across the coding tools I use. Imagine asking a coding agent to fix a small bug. It fixes the bug, but also renames a few files and tidies up code you weren’t asking it to change. You explain: “Please stop tidying unrelated files. Keep edits focused on the task I asked for.” The agent adjusts. You get the smaller change you wanted and carry on. That correction did something useful. It explained how you want to work together. I want that effort to keep being useful when I start another conversation, open another project, or use a different coding tool. That is the idea behind Tuna : turn useful corrections into preferences that can travel between my coding agents. I’ve built an early version for OpenCode, Copilot CLI, Codex, and Claude Code. It listens for new messages, identifies feedback worth keeping, and maintains shared instructions those tools can read. The interesting part is deciding what deserves to survive. Remembering every sentence would create a different problem. A useful memory has to preserve what I meant, including when it applies, and let me change my mind. A correction has two jobs The immediate job of our correction is to fix the current interaction: undo the unrelated changes and finish the bug fix. Its second job could be to improve the next interaction: when I ask for a small change, keep the work focused. For a coding agent, those jobs happen through different mechanisms. During a conversation, the model receives messages and other information the application supplies. That information is its context . A correction included in that context can influence what it does next. For a future session to benefit, something needs to carry the useful part forward. That could be a saved instruction, a memory feature, or a tool the agent calls to retrieve a preference. The model agreeing with me in one reply doesn’t, by itself, establish which of those things happened. This distinction shaped what I wanted to build. Tuna saves guidance that can be supplied in later sessions. It does not retrain the underlying model. The mechanism is closer to keeping a small set of working agreements and bringing them to the next conversation. In our example, the agreement might be: That sentence is much more useful to a future agent than replaying the whole argument about which files should have been renamed. Put the agreement somewhere it survives The obvious first step is to write the agreement down myself. Coding tools already have places for persistent instructions. Codex reads AGENTS.md files, for example, combining personal guidance with instructions from the project. A simple file could contain: This is a good foundation: plain text I can read, edit, and keep. But it leaves me with a maintenance job. I have to recognise which corrections are reusable, remember to write them down, avoid repeating myself, and update them when they stop being useful. There is existing work here too. Claude Code’s auto memory can save preferences and feedback between sessions. Copilot Memory includes both repository facts and personal preferences. Persistent memory is already part of how coding tools are evolving. The question I wanted to explore with Tuna is what happens across those tools. If I explain how I like an agent to work in one application, I would like that preference to be available when I use another. I also want to inspect the particular correction behind it and remove it without needing to remember where each tool stores its own notes. That gave me a concrete direction: a shared collection of personal preferences, with a readable instruction file as one way to deliver them. It also set a boundary. Tuna’s shared preferences are about how I want agents to work. A particular project’s architecture, a task’s acceptance criteria, and someone else’s preferences do not automatically belong in that collection. Decide which messages are actually feedback Once I start listening to conversations, I have a selection problem. Most messages are not lasting preferences. “Add a settings page” is a new task. “The app crashes when I click Save” is a bug report. “Use a blue background for this demo” is a requirement for one piece of work. Turning those into global instructions would make later sessions worse. Even frustration isn’t enough. “This is frustrating” tells me the result was disappointing, but doesn’t tell me what the agent should do differently next time. On the other hand, a polite correction can be precise: “For small bug fixes, skip the long recap. Give me a short summary.” There is a useful preference there, and its condition matters. A detailed architecture review might still be exactly what I want. I made this distinction the first job of Tuna’s analysis. It asks a model to identify durable, actionable corrections about how the agent should work. It asks it to leave ordinary requests, quoted complaints, and one-off requirements alone. Quotation is another easy trap. If I ask what someone meant by “never write tests,” I’m discussing their words. That sentence should not become my preference. These examples are deliberately small, but they expose a difficult judgment. The same words can mean different things depending on what happened before them. “Keep it short” might refer to a reply, a function, or a timeout. Tuna includes recent assistant context when the integration can provide it, so the analyst has more than an isolated sentence to work with. That context helps interpret the correction. It doesn’t get to become evidence that I said something I never said. Keep the reason beside the rule A list of instructions without their origins would be hard to trust. If Tuna decides that I dislike a certain approach, I want to be able to ask: what did I actually say? So a learned note contains both a short instruction and an exact quotation supporting it. It also records where the feedback came from: the coding tool, session, time, and source model when that information is available. A simplified example of a stored note looks like this. The ID and conversation details are illustrative: A harness is the application running the coding agent: the part that manages the conversation, tools, and model calls. OpenCode and Copilot CLI are examples. The model that responds inside the harness is a separate choice. The distinction matters in the note above. model: "unknown" means the integration did not provide the model’s identity. Tuna doesn’t ask its analyst to guess one. The model doing the analysis might also be different from the model that originally received my feedback. I added a concrete check around the quotation: it must occur exactly in the user’s message. An invented quotation causes analysis to fail, and the messages stay queued for another attempt. The implementation also checks that the referenced message exists and that the category is recognised. This helps make the result inspectable, but it doesn’t prove the interpretation is right. A model could quote me accurately and still turn a narrow request into an overbroad rule. Retaining the words makes that mistake easier to find and correct. There is another distinction worth preserving: where feedback came from is not automatically where it applies . A preference expressed in Codex might be useful everywhere. If I explicitly limit it to a certain situation or model, that condition needs to stay in the instruction itself. Get it into the next conversation Now I have a message and a possible preference. How does it reach the next agent? I split the work into capture, analysis, and publishing instructions. Capture happens through a hook: a small integration the coding tool calls when I submit a prompt. Its job is to pass the message to Tuna’s local queue and let the coding session continue. It does not wait for a model to decide what the message means. Analysis happens in the background. By default, Tuna checks for a batch every 30 seconds. It asks a supported, already-installed coding harness to run the preference analysis, using that harness’s authentication and model. A useful correction becomes a stored note. A message with no reusable preference produces no note. Publishing instructions happens separately. Tuna gathers the relevant notes, reconciles them, and refreshes the shared instruction file. It calls this step consolidation . It runs daily at 23:00 local time while the service is running, or I can request it immediately: This distinction is useful when inspecting the tool. A preference can already exist in the local database and be available to query before it has been written into the shared file. “Tuna saved a note” and “my next session loaded that note as an instruction” are different events. The default shared file is /.agents/AGENTS.md. Tuna links each configured tool’s global instruction path to it. A symlink is a filesystem link: several paths lead to the same file, rather than separate copies that need to be kept in sync. Following our opening correction through to the file, suppose I already have one hand-written instruction: “Explain important trade-offs.” After consolidation, the file could look like this: The original instruction stays. The correction becomes a line in Tuna’s marked section, linked to the note we saw earlier by tuna:12. When another configured tool loads this file, that guidance is available alongside my hand-written instructions. For example, these default paths lead to that shared file after setup: During setup, Tuna preserves and merges existing instruction contents, and backs up the files it replaces with links. New sessions pick up the configured hooks and instructions according to the tool’s own loading behavior. Updating a file doesn’t imply that every already-open conversation immediately rereads it. The shared file is also guidance, not an enforcement mechanism. A project can have more specific instructions, a tool can have overriding configuration, and a model can still misapply what it reads. Tuna makes the preference available; whether that improves the work remains something to evaluate. A memory needs to change with me Saving every useful correction still isn’t enough. Over time, I will repeat myself. “Keep edits focused on the requested task” and “avoid unrelated changes” express the same preference. Keeping a newer representative is more useful than accumulating every phrasing. I may also change my mind. Suppose I first ask for completion summaries in paragraphs, then later say that I prefer bullet points. Keeping both instructions leaves the next agent with an avoidable contradiction. But “the newest instruction wins” is too crude. “Keep small bug-fix summaries short” and “explain architectural trade-offs in detail” can both be right. They describe different situations. This is why consolidation does more than append a new line. I ask the analyst to keep distinct preferences, choose the newer representative of a duplicate, and resolve genuine conflicts using the latest applicable correction. Different conditions and model-specific guidance should stay separate. The model returns the IDs of notes to keep, and Tuna rebuilds the learned section from those notes. Each published line keeps its note marker. That connection lets Tuna remove the particular rule later, instead of having to guess which sentence came from which correction. Existing hand-written instructions need attention too. If the file already says “write paragraph summaries” and the newest correction says “use bullet points,” appending another section hasn’t resolved the disagreement. The implementation lets the analyst propose exact-text edits to existing instructions when a retained preference justifies reconciling a duplicate or conflict. It asks the analyst to preserve unrelated text. Tuna checks that each edit names a retained note and that the text being replaced occurs exactly once. It also checks whether the file changed while analysis was running, so a concurrent manual edit causes it to stop and retry rather than overwrite that newer file. Changed instruction files are backed up. These checks make the operation more controlled, but the meaning of a proposed edit is still a model judgment. Inspecting the result remains part of understanding whether the idea works. Make forgetting an ordinary operation I don’t want a mistaken inference to become a permanent working agreement. Inspecting and removing preferences need to be normal parts of using Tuna. I can look at recent notes or search for a particular subject: The category narrows the kind of preference; --json gives an agent or script structured results. The example notes in this article use invented IDs. In a real session I would use the ID shown by my own list or query output: Removal clears that note’s supporting quotation and removes its published line. The ID and removed status remain available in the history. It does not erase previous file backups or reverse an earlier edit to a hand-written instruction, so those are separate things to inspect if I need to undo more than the learned line. Tuna also has an age limit. By default, notes older than 180 days are excluded during consolidation. An old preference doesn’t necessarily stay useful forever, and repeating a correction can supply a newer note. I can change the age limit, or turn it off: This is an age-based policy, not evidence that a preference became wrong on a particular birthday. Choosing a good default—and making stale guidance visible—is part of the design I still want to learn from. Agents can retrieve preferences directly too. Tuna exposes preferences, list, and remove through MCP , a standard way for an agent application to call external tools. They can also use the command line. That makes the note collection available on demand as well as through the instruction file. Keep the listener out of the way For this to be useful, remembering feedback must not make every conversation feel slower or more fragile. I made capture bounded and silent. If Tuna is stopped, the hook does nothing useful and the coding session can continue. If a model call fails after a message has reached the queue, that message stays pending. tuna status reports the problem, with diagnostics in the service log. There is a subtle loop to avoid as well: Tuna uses a coding harness to analyse messages from coding harnesses. Without a boundary, its analysis prompts could look like more material to capture. The analysis runs in its own working directory, carries an internal marker, and sets a flag that capture recognises and skips. The harness-specific invocation restricts tools and disables Tuna integrations where supported. The analyst’s task is to return structured data about the supplied messages. The current implementation is a Go command-line program with a background service and a local SQLite database. Communication with the service uses a user-private Unix socket—a local connection on the machine—rather than a public listening network port. “Local” here describes the queue, notes, and instruction files. The selected harness sends analysis to its model provider using the normal authentication and usage allowance. It does not mean the inference happens offline. After successful analysis, Tuna clears the queued raw message payloads. Retained notes keep the relevant supporting quotation. It starts observing new prompts after setup; it does not go back through all my historical conversations. It also only sees what the integrations expose, so a thumbs-down reaction in a UI is not automatically captured as feedback. Those limits matter to the experience. The tool should make it possible to explain what it saw, what it retained, and how that became an instruction. What I have built so far The capture, analysis, query, consolidation, and removal paths described here are implemented. The current release targets macOS and Linux on ARM64 and AMD64, and expects an installed, authenticated supported coding harness to provide the analysis model. The installation instructions cover direct downloads and installation through my Binzo tool. Once the binary is installed: start installs integrations for supported tools it finds on the executable search path, links their global instructions, and starts the background service. Codex requires trusting the new hook in /hooks. The integrations need hooks-capable versions; the OpenCode integration targets V2. If I want an installed and signed-in Copilot CLI to provide the analysis, I can choose it explicitly. I can also change the daily refresh time: Without an explicit choice, Tuna selects the first installed CLI in the order Copilot, OpenCode, Claude, then Codex. Installed doesn’t necessarily mean signed in, so status is useful when the first available tool cannot complete analysis. The service runs until I stop it or the machine shuts down. I currently need to start it again after a reboot. Reads of the saved notes work while it is stopped; capture, removal, and consolidation need the running service. I added tests around things I want to remain dependable: rejecting invented quotations, retaining messages after failed analysis, preserving existing setup, removing published rules, and refusing to overwrite an instruction file that changed during consolidation. Those tests use fake analysis outputs. They check what the program does with an answer; they don’t establish how often a real model interprets a correction correctly. That is a different question, and probably the most important one. What I want to find out next The question I care about is whether this reduces the effort of working with agents over time. More stored notes would be a poor measure on its own. I want to find out whether the next agent actually makes fewer of the mistakes I have already corrected. Whether switching tools preserves useful working agreements. Whether the saved rule still means what I meant when I gave the feedback. There are several ways this could go wrong. A project-specific request could become a global preference. A conditional rule could lose its condition. A new correction could be treated as a contradiction when it really describes an exception. A preference could be saved correctly but never loaded by the session that needs it. That is why I keep coming back to the link between a message, a note, and a published instruction. Each step should be understandable, and each retained preference should be something I can inspect and change. Tuna is an experiment in making that loop useful: I explain how I want to work, the tool keeps the reusable part, and a later conversation starts with a little more of that understanding already available. Notes and further reading This write-up describes my implementation at 24 September 2026. The conversations and note IDs are illustrative examples. I’ve linked the parts of the code behind the main design decisions: - Capture and the context passed with a message - The analysis instructions and evidence checks - Consolidation, instruction updates, and removal - Linking instructions and installing integrations - Building and contributing The Claude Code memory documentation, Copilot Memory overview, and Codex instruction-file guide provide useful context for the existing approaches I’m working alongside.

docs.title: The Speed of Prototyping in the Age of AI
docs.body: Note: These are personal reflections on how my workflow has shifted over the past year, not a pitch for any tool. Your mileage will (and probably should) vary. A few years back I wrote about my love of throwaway prototypes; those little proof-of-concepts that exist purely to get an idea out of your head and into something tangible. At the time, my biggest bottleneck was me ; the time it took to scaffold a project, wire up the boring bits, and get to a place where the interesting parts could actually be tested. Fast forward to now, and that bottleneck has all but vanished. I've been a little hesitant to write about this. I've already shared some cautious thoughts on AI and where it fits into my workflow, and I stand by all of it. I still think the industry is figuring things out in real time, and I still think it pays to be careful. But cautious doesn't mean blind, and the honest truth is that AI has changed how quickly I can go from "I wonder if…" to "oh, it works" . The recent repos If you've looked at my GitHub recently, you'll have noticed a stream of new repos showing up. Sakoa, a progressive systems language I've been designing from scratch, complete with an effect system, three memory modes, and a MIR with multiple backends. Kato, a notation language meant to sit somewhere between JSON, TOML, and YAML, but explicitly designed to be friendly to both humans and agents. Seal, a tiny CLI that quietly kills the .env file by stashing secrets in OS-native credential stores. Karabiner, an iOS-first agent-native messaging app. Plim, a Notion-inspired, embeddable block editor for the web with a framework-agnostic core and React bindings. And a few more knocking around that aren't ready for the spotlight yet. A few years ago, that list would have been three repos with READMEs, two abandoned branches, and one working prototype I'd be quietly proud of. Now? The prototypes exist . They run. Some of them have tests. A couple are starting to look like real projects. And while not all of them will turn into anything serious (and that's kind of the point), there is something really satisfying about being able to actually try an idea, rather than just talk about it. Zooming out The thing nobody really warned me about is how much AI changes the shape of engineering work, not just the speed of it. When I'm not the one typing every line, I'm forced to think differently. I'm thinking about boundaries, contracts, and how the pieces fit together. I'm writing prompts and specs that describe the system holistically, before the system exists. That shift sounds small but it's been quietly transformative. I'm planning at a more abstracted level, framing problems before I solve them, and I've gotten noticeably better at delegating; both to agents and to people. Turns out that the skill of "describing exactly what success looks like, in a way that a junior engineer (or a model) can act on without you in the room" is the same skill in both directions. Sharing vision, breaking work down, anticipating where things might go wrong; these are muscles I've been forced to exercise much more deliberately, and I'm better for it. On productivity I've been tracking this loosely for a while, mostly out of curiosity.
